analysis.one_liner: Gives workers and retirees higher priority in business bankruptcies and limits executive pay when labor concessions are made.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite bankruptcy rules so that when a company goes bankrupt, employees and retirees are paid ahead of more of their wages, benefits, and severance. It would cap executive bonuses and pay packages during bankruptcy, let companies reject union contracts only after strict good-faith bargaining, force courts to weigh job preservation when approving reorganization plans, and let pension participants claim shortfalls when their plan is terminated. It also bans company executives from keeping enhanced retirement packages when they have terminated the workers' pension plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of companies in bankruptcy: they would recover up to $20,000 in unpaid wages and benefit contributions ahead of most other creditors, collect severance pay, claim losses from employer stock in their retirement accounts where the employer committed fraud, and file claims for pension shortfalls. Union members would gain new bargaining protections, and retirees would keep health benefits unless strict standards were met.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority cap on unpaid wages and benefit-plan contributions from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker, and removes the 180-day filing window so workers are not cut off by timing rules [S3].
Lets workers claim the lost value of employer stock in their 401(k)-style accounts as a priority claim when the employer committed fraud or breached a duty to the plan [S3].

Bars executive bonuses and pay enhancements during bankruptcy unless a court finds them reasonable and not disproportionate to concessions the nonmanagement workforce made, and lets the estate claw back a share of executive pay when workers' contracts or retiree benefits were cut [S3].

Requires companies to negotiate in good faith and seek only minimal savings before a court can let them reject a union contract or cut retiree health benefits, and gives unions the right to strike or seek arbitration if the contract is rejected [S3].

Requires bankruptcy courts to weigh job preservation, retiree health, and defined-benefit pensions when choosing between reorganization plans and approving asset sales, and charges $20,000 per retiree against asset-sale proceeds to fund a year of replacement health coverage when retiree benefits are cut [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Bankrupt companies' estates, their secured lenders (who would recover less because workers' claims jump ahead), and executives and consultants, whose bonuses, pay enhancements, and pre-bankruptcy transfers could be blocked or clawed back. Companies might also face higher borrowing costs if lenders price in the larger priority claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lenders, executives, and bankrupt companies' estates

drawbacks.text: Secured lenders recover less in bankruptcies because wages, benefits, and severance would jump ahead of them and could be deducted even when a lender has waived that right by agreement; lenders could respond by charging struggling firms more or lending less, making turnarounds harder [S3].

The rules on rejecting union contracts and cutting retiree benefits are strict: proposals are limited to minimal savings for two years, and courts must weigh the effect of a strike, which could make reorganizations slower, more litigious, or more likely to end in liquidation [S3].
Buyers of assets from bankrupt companies would be charged $20,000 per retiree whose benefits are cut, a cost that could reduce bids and sale proceeds for other creditors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and retirees, the gains are substantial: bankruptcy currently falls hardest on them because they cannot diversify their stake in one employer, as the bill's own findings state [S3]. The costs fall on lenders and executives, who would recover less, and potentially on distressed firms through costlier credit. The bill is deliberately aggressive; a fair objection is that tilting the bargaining table toward labor could occasionally push a struggling company into liquidation instead of reorganization. On balance the bill shifts bankruptcy's losses from people who earned their benefits over a lifetime toward creditors and executives who can absorb the loss.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Durbin introduced the bill on September 25, 2007, joined by Senators Kennedy, Feingold, and Obama [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; that was its last recorded action [S5].
The committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bankrupt companies, their secured lenders, and executives whose pay and deferred compensation would have faced new limits keep the bankruptcy rules as they were; workers and retirees lost a chance at stronger claims and negotiating rights.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders and corporate executives in bankruptcy

for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction in the Senate [S3].

sides.party_line_note: All twelve Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows where opponents stood [S4].

industries.industry: Secured lenders and other senior creditors
industries.note: Workers' wage, benefit, and severance claims would be paid ahead of them and could be charged against collateral even where lenders had waived such charges, shrinking their recovery in bankruptcies.

Bonuses and pay enhancements during bankruptcy would be barred or capped, executive retirement plans could not be assumed if the workers' pension was terminated, and transfers to insiders and consultants made within a year of bankruptcy could be clawed back.

Stricter rules on rejecting union contracts and cutting retiree benefits could lengthen and complicate reorganizations, though a stated purpose of the bill is keeping companies operating and preserving jobs rather than liquidating.
Unions could file claims on behalf of members, gain good-faith bargaining requirements and strike rights before contract rejection, and have their legal fees paid by the debtor.
